summary: Some networks, such as those carrying financial market data, care about performance measures like latency as much as other path constraints. This document extends PCEP so such service-related metrics can be requested, and used when computing label switched paths.

eli5.summary: Sometimes the fastest route matters more than the shortest one. This lets a path planner be told what really matters, such as speed, when choosing a route.

subtitle: PCEP learns to ask for paths by latency, delay variation, packet loss and link utilization, not just cost.

tldr.problem: Some networks, such as financial data networks, must pick paths by performance measures like latency tied to a Service Level Agreement, but PCEP had no standard way to ask for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds six METRIC types for path delay, delay variation and loss (point-to-point and point-to-multipoint), a new BU object that caps link bandwidth utilization, and three new objective functions, plus the error handling for PCEs that cannot do it.
tldr.outcome: A client can bound or optimize a path by these measures, and a PCE can report the values it computed or the constraint it could not meet. RFC 9756 later updated this document.

today: RFC 8233 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Paths Need Performance Constraints
sections.content:
In some networks, for example financial information networks such as stock market data providers, network performance criteria like latency are as critical to path selection as other metrics and constraints. These measures come from the Service Level Agreement (SLA) between customers and providers. Link bandwidth utilization, meaning how much of a link is actually carrying traffic, is another factor.

The pieces already existed. The OSPF and IS-IS TE Metric Extensions (RFC 7471 and RFC 7810) put link latency, delay variation, loss and utilized bandwidth into the Traffic Engineering Database, and RFC 6374 describes how to measure them in MPLS networks. What was missing was a way for a Path Computation Client (PCC) to ask a Path Computation Element (PCE) for a path that meets such criteria. This document extends PCEP (RFC 5440) to carry latency, delay variation, packet loss and link bandwidth utilization as constraints for end-to-end path computation.
sections.eli5: Some customers care a lot about how quickly data arrives. The planner already knew the numbers for each road, but nobody could ask it to use them.

sections.title: New METRIC Types for Delay, Variation and Loss
sections.content:
PCEP's existing METRIC object carries a metric value, a type field (T) and flag bits including B and P. The RFC defines six new types: T=12 Path Delay, T=13 Path Delay Variation, T=14 Path Loss, and T=15, 16 and 17 for the point-to-multipoint (P2MP) versions.

Each path metric is built from the per-link values advertised by the IGP. Path Delay is the sum of the link delays, and Path Delay Variation is the sum of the links' average delay variation, though an implementation MAY use an enhanced composition function. Path Loss combines the fractional loss of each link as (1 - ((1-FL(Lp1)) * (1-FL(Lp2)) * .. * (1-FL(LpK)))) * 100, as a percentage. For P2MP trees, each metric is the maximum over all destinations, so it reflects the destination with the worst value.

Delay and delay variation are in microseconds and loss is a percentage, all encoded in the 32-bit IEEE floating point format that the METRIC object uses. The IGP carries these values in a 24-bit field, so conversion could introduce some loss of precision.

A PCC MAY put these metrics in a Path Computation Request (PCReq). With the B bit set, the value is a bound that the path must not exceed. With the B bit cleared, the PCC is asking the PCE to optimize that measure. A PCE MAY use them in a reply (PCRep) to report the computed value, or alongside a NO-PATH object when it cannot meet the constraint. How the PCE computes the path is outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: You can say 'get me there in at most this long' or 'make it as quick as you can'. The planner can answer with how long its route will take, or say it could not find one that fast.

sections.title: When a PCE Cannot or Will Not Comply
sections.content:
Not every PCE will support these metrics, so the P bit in the METRIC header decides what happens. If the PCE does not understand the new type and the P bit is clear, it SHOULD ignore the object. If the P bit is set and the PCE does not understand it, the PCE MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 4 (Not supported object) and Error-value 4 (Unsupported parameter).

Two new error values were created. If the PCE understands the type but does not support it and the P bit is set, it MUST send Error-Type 4 with Error-value 5 (Unsupported network performance constraint), and the request is canceled. If local policy forbids such constraints, it MUST send Error-Type 5 (Policy violation) with Error-value 8 (Not allowed network performance constraint). The BU object follows the same pattern.
sections.eli5: If the planner does not know how to do what you asked, it tells you why, or just skips that part when you said it was optional.

sections.title: Bandwidth Utilization and the BU Object
sections.content:
Two utilization measures are defined. Link Bandwidth Utilization (LBU) is utilized bandwidth divided by maximum bandwidth, times 100, and covers both RSVP-TE and non-RSVP-TE traffic. Link Reserved Bandwidth Utilization (LRBU) counts only RSVP-TE LSPs: reserved bandwidth utilization is utilized bandwidth minus (residual bandwidth minus available bandwidth), shown as a percentage of maximum reservable bandwidth.

A new BU object (Object-Class 35, Object-Type 1) states the upper limit of acceptable link utilization. Its body has a 24-bit reserved field, an 8-bit Type (1 for LBU, 2 for LRBU) and a 32-bit Bandwidth Utilization percentage in IEEE floating point format, for a fixed length of 8 bytes. A PCE that supports it MUST ensure that no link on the computed path exceeds the given LBU or LRBU percentage.

A PCReq or PCRep MAY carry several BU objects if each has a different type; for a repeated type, the first is processed and later ones are ignored. In an unsuccessful reply, a PCE MAY include a BU object with a NO-PATH object to show which constraint failed. Use of the BU object for P2MP LSPs is outside the scope.
sections.eli5: This is a rule that says 'do not send me down any road that is already more than this full'.

sections.title: New Objective Functions
sections.content:
An objective function (OF) tells the PCE what to optimize. Delay and delay variation can keep using the existing Minimum Cost Path function from RFC 5541. For the other goals the RFC adds three codes: MPLP (code 9) finds the path that minimizes the path loss; MUP (code 10) maximizes the minimum, over the links of the path, of the fraction of maximum bandwidth still unused; and MRUP (code 11) does the same for reservable bandwidth that is not yet used by reservations.

If a PCE does not know or support an objective function defined here, it follows the procedure in Section 3.1 of RFC 5541.
sections.eli5: Besides 'shortest', you can now ask for 'least bumpy' or 'least crowded'. The crowded one picks the route whose busiest road is still the emptiest.

sections.title: Messages, Stateful PCE and Reoptimization
sections.content:
The PCReq and PCRep message formats are updated with RBNF. Requests may now include a list of BU objects beside the existing metric list, and replies may include them in the attribute list. The PCRpt message, used by a PCC in the stateful model of RFC 8231, can carry a BU object to show the limit the PCC set when it delegated an LSP to an active stateful PCE. A stateful PCE MAY also use the PCReq and PCRep extensions in passive operation.

For inter-domain paths, the new metrics apply to end-to-end computation like existing IGP or TE metrics, and the BU object acts like a METRIC with the B bit set. All domains should have the same understanding of the metrics, otherwise some form of metric normalization from RFC 5441 MUST be applied.

For reoptimization, a PCC that sees performance degrade against its constraint, either by measurement as in RFC 6374 or by watching the TED, MAY ask the PCE to reoptimize by sending a PCReq with the R bit set in the RP object. A stateful PCE can decide on its own which LSPs to reoptimize, for example when a link's loss rises.
sections.eli5: If the road gets slower than you were promised, you can ask the planner to find a better route.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the new METRIC types, BU object and OF codes add no new security concerns beyond those of RFC 5440 and RFC 5541 in themselves. It adds that delay and loss data can be sensitive in some deployments, could be used to influence path computation and setup with adverse effect, and that snooping on PCEP messages or using them for reconnaissance may reveal sensitive information about the network.

Such deployments should use suitable PCEP security mechanisms, such as the TCP Authentication Option (TCP-AO) or the TLS-based PCEPS work, which the RFC considers better suited to this sensitive information.
sections.eli5: Knowing which roads are slow or busy is useful to a bad guy, so the messages should be locked up.

items.label: Path Delay
items.desc: Sum of link delays, in microseconds.

items.label: Path Delay Variation
items.desc: Sum of link average delay variation, in microseconds.

items.label: Path Loss
items.desc: End-to-end packet loss as a percentage.

items.label: P2MP Path Delay
items.desc: Worst path delay among all tree destinations.

items.label: P2MP Path Delay Variation
items.desc: Worst delay variation among all tree destinations.

items.label: P2MP Path Loss
items.desc: Worst packet loss among all tree destinations.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Bandwidth utilization type: 1 is LBU, 2 is LRBU.

fields.name: Bandwidth Utilization
fields.desc: Percentage in IEEE floating point format.

items.label: MPLP
items.desc: Minimum Packet Loss Path: minimize the path loss.

items.label: MUP
items.desc: Maximum Under-Utilized Path: maximize the least unused fraction of maximum bandwidth.

items.label: MRUP
items.desc: Maximum Reserved Under-Utilized Path: maximize the least unused fraction of reservable bandwidth.
